claims.claim: A 2009 Journal of Money, Credit and Banking paper finds federal funds futures premiums have often been negative since 2000, and argues that zero average forecast errors and survey proxies can bias premium estimates.

claims.supporting_quote: We propose a new method to estimate the premiums and find that the premiums have been often negative since 2000, which is generally consistent with the negative betas observed in the 2000s.

claims.claim: Options on federal funds futures began trading in March 2003, and a 2005 Journal of Futures Markets paper shows the implied PDF of discrete FOMC outcomes can be recovered with ordinary least squares.
claims.episode_span: Options on federal funds futures began trading in March 2003.
claims.source_title: Recovering market expectations of FOMC rate changes with options on federal funds futures
claims.supporting_quote: This article demonstrates how options on federal funds futures, which began trading in March 2003, can be used to recover the implied probability density function (PDF) for future Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) interest‐rate outcomes.

claims.claim: A 2016 FEDS Note examines front-end term premiums using federal funds futures and the Desk’s sell-side and buy-side surveys in order to extract probabilities of a rate hike.
claims.episode_span: It uses federal funds futures together with the Desk’s Survey of Primary Dealers and its Survey of Market Participants
claims.source_title: Front-End Term Premiums in Federal Funds Futures Rates and Implied Probabilities of Future Rate Hikes
claims.supporting_quote: In this note, we examine empirical evidence on term premiums at the very front end, utilizing federal funds futures data as well as responses to the Desk's sell-side survey (Survey of Primary Dealers, or PD survey) and buy-side survey (Survey of Market Participants), and discuss plausible front-end term premium assumptions that one can use to extract probabilities of a rate hike at upcoming meetings from market quotes.
